answer:
So we’ve been tracking Monday for quite some time on SaaStr.  It was one of our first true “SaaS success stories” — and it’s become a great case study in going more enterprise.
It IPO’d just as Covid hit in March 2020, which made things … interesting.  But then they exploded into growth in late 2020-early 2021, fueled by work-from-home and digital transformation.  And while that slowed down later in 2022, Monday has still held up well to many other public B2B leaders, growing 33% last year despite macro headwinds.
And now?  Now it’s crossing $500m+ in ARR!
How did this Israeli-born company do it?
A few learnings:
#1.  Go Upmarket Earlier Than You Think.  They Did This Around $100M in ARR
.  Monday started off SMB but went fairly quickly very enterprise, with its largest customers paying hundreds of thousands or even millions a year.   This is something I learned myself after building several products ourselves.  If you go very truly SMB, you’ll get stuck there unless you are truly dominant (e.g., Shopify).  Even if your product seems like it should be truly SMB, going upmarket earlier often can be a good strategy.  It can add an extra layer of revenue to keep you growing faster than purely SMB alone.  Zoom did it, too, although it took them until almost $400m in ARR to really tap their larger customer base.  Asana waited longer — until around $200m ARR.  But it worked much better for Monday.  It also works better when you have strong brand pull in bigger enterprises.

Dear SaaStr:  How Can I Really Stand Out During an Interview? Here are my Top Tips:
Do your research before you walk into any interview. Go on their website and learn what they do and who else is there that does it better than you. Then go back through all those names and send them an email with why you’d be great at working with/for them.
The #1 thing most people fail at during interviews is not doing this. They don’t know enough about the company or the role beforehand. If you can show up prepared and share specific reasons why you’re interested in working with someone, especially if they’re considered top talent, you’ll stand out immediately. The fact that you took time to understand who they are and how you could contribute shows initiative and dedication – qualities employers always want to see. This alone often gets you hired over other candidates that seem “better” but lack preparation. It’s also a great way to start building relationships within the organization, which is essential for long-term success. Second, tailor your responses specifically to each role and opportunity. Instead of generic answers about leadership skills or teamwork, focus on how your unique experience applies directly to the position. For example, if you’re interviewing for a sales leadership role, highlight specific examples of how you’ve built high-performing teams in the past and explain exactly how you would apply those strategies in this new context. Tailoring your approach demonstrates that you understand the nuances of each opportunity and have thoughtfully considered how you fit in.

So with public SaaS multiples crashing from 30x+ ARR to less than 10x for many leaders (more on that
here
), it’s natural investors are worried about their investments — and the ones they might make.
It makes sense:
A VC fund is only as good as its exits, ideally at least one or two unicorns per $100m-$200m fund.  And if you’re not raising more capital yourself each year, your ability to generate those unicorn level returns … is limited by how fast valuations go up.
If valuations continue to fall, then we’ll be back to 2017-like days where most VC funds can’t even pay out all the carry to their partners.
And so I get worried when I see folks being overly stressed about “multiple compression” now. Yes, yes, yes. If times don’t change, things will just keep going down, down, down for a while.
But here’s what I’ve learned over time investing and working with startups:
There are basically three types of companies, in terms of revenue growth rate and multiple:
Type #1: Growing Quickly AND Trading At High Multiple
These are unicorns today, but were pre-IPO decacorns before Covid. They have high NRR, often >120%, strong gross margins, and grow quickly enough to trade at premium prices. In general, these are worth it, because they also tend to stay valuable longer. The best Type#1s can become Type#2s after IPOs, which really do compound into billion dollar businesses, if not always in nominal dollars. But there aren’t too many of them. Usually just 5%-8% of any given batch of start-ups.

answer:
So there’s an interesting dynamic with SaaS companies that have strong recurring revenue.  I’ve invested in several at $1m+ ARR, and all but one had at least 100% NRR for years.
Then they got acquired for less than their next year run-rate:
The point is if you are growing quickly enough (even just 50%), then your customers will be happy, even if your product isn’t quite as good as it could be today — or ever was.  But not forever.  Sooner or later, you’ll cross the line from being a high-growth start-up into being a low growth, high retention “NRR Zombie”.  And you can’t hide here, folks.  You won’t get acquired, you won’t attract top talent, etc. etc.  Your investors may still give you some extra time, if you were early-stage when this happened.  But it’s tough times once you cross over from High Growth / Happy Customer mode to Low Growth / High Retention mode.
What should you do?
First, don’t quit.  There’s always another act in many B2B businesses.  Many more than we realize until we look back.
Second, go meet every customer.  Every month.  Every quarter, ideally.
Third, find new markets to sell into.  New use cases for existing products.  Even if your core market is saturated, expand beyond it.
Fourth, make sure you have great second-order revenue motions working, too
.  That often means having multiple sales reps per account, closing upsell deals faster than you close initial ones, etc.
Fifth, ask yourself honestly if it’s really worth continuing
.  If you think you can scale up again, maybe.  Otherwise, sometimes it makes sense to shut down.  Especially if you raised VC capital.

This route requires patience because these investors often only invest once every few months. It also increases the risk that you could end up overfunded—something many founders aren’t prepared for. If you choose this path, make sure you have a clear plan to spend the capital efficiently while still delivering the growth required to return value to investors. The Second Choice — Wait Until Metrics Are Stronger
If you don’t feel comfortable going down the “non-fundable” route, focus on improving your fundamentals first. A lot of VCs today prefer Series B investments where revenue has already crossed $10-20 million and there are strong unit economics in place.

not spending any more than you bring in each month
. Sounds simple, but too many founders just don’t follow this rule. They hire another VP they aren’t sure will work out. Or upgrade their laptop with an even fancier model than last year’s. . This sounds silly, but it isn’t. It doesn’t need to be yourself or an accountant — although those would both work well. Just pick someone who has managed budgets before (or wants to learn) and get them to review every single expense. Every vendor, every credit card bill, everything. There may be nothing better than a CFO reviewing expenses line by line … even if she was never a “people person”. If someone else reviews every expense, no matter how small, you’ll spend less. Because you won’t be able to justify so much stuff anymore. In my case, after we ran out of money at $5m ARR, I hired a COO that used to run finance for Yahoo!. He saved us from going under.
He reviewed
every
expense. Including ones that looked like they came from a different company. We did lose him to a hot start-up, but he got us through the tough times. It took me far longer to realize why his help here mattered so much. His job wasn’t to build processes, nor to own product strategy, nor to improve sales scripts.
